questions.stem: Which of the following is the average-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.explanation: Quicksort's average-case time complexity is $O(n \\log n)$ because, on average, the partitioning process divides the array into two roughly equal halves, leading to a balanced recursion tree. This results in a logarithmic number of levels, each requiring linear work to partition, hence $O(n \\log n)$. The most tempting wrong option, $O(n^2)$, represents the worst-case scenario, not the average case.

questions.stem: Given an array of 1000 elements, what is the expected number of comparisons in quicksort in the average case? Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: The average number of comparisons in quicksort is approximately $C(n) = 2n \log n$. For $n = 1000$, $C(1000) \approx 2 \times 1000 \times 10 = 20000$ comparisons.

markingGuide: Mention the decision tree model of sorting.

questions.stem: Which pivot choice strategy can help maintain $O(n \log n)$ performance in quicksort?

options.text: Choose the median of the array.

questions.explanation: Choosing the median of the array as the pivot helps maintain $O(n \\log n)$ performance in quicksort because it ensures that the partitioning step divides the array into two equal halves. This balanced division minimizes the depth of the recursion tree, leading to optimal performance. Choosing the first or last element can lead to unbalanced partitions, especially in sorted or nearly sorted arrays, degrading performance to $O(n^2)$.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.explanation: The worst-case time complexity of quicksort is $O(n^2)$, which occurs when the pivot choice results in highly unbalanced partitions, such as when the smallest or largest element is consistently chosen as the pivot. This leads to a recursion tree with $n$ levels, each requiring linear work, hence $O(n^2)$. The option $O(n \\log n)$ is incorrect for the worst case, as it represents the average-case complexity.

questions.stem: Describe how quicksort's partitioning process works with an example.
markingGuide: Explain how elements are rearranged around the pivot.
questions.explanation: The partitioning process involves selecting a pivot and rearranging elements so that those less than the pivot are on the left, and those greater are on the right. For example, with the array [4, 5, 3, 7, 2], choosing 4 as the pivot results in [3, 2, 4, 7, 5].

questions.stem: True or False: Quicksort's average-case complexity is better than its worst-case complexity.
questions.explanation: The statement is true because quicksort's average-case complexity is $O(n \\log n)$, which is more efficient than its worst-case complexity of $O(n^2)$. In the average case, the pivot choice leads to balanced partitions, while in the worst case, poor pivot choices result in unbalanced partitions, increasing the number of comparisons needed.
